# Library semantics are data the analysis derives from decompiled code

Phase 5a described libraries in a table of C# families, one hand-written entry per overload, chosen
by a census of the calls the demo and the corpora make. It could not keep up with the ecosystem, and
it could not say the thing that mattered most. On eShop, 132 of the 142 semantic gaps after phase 5b
are calls that take a delegate: LINQ with lambdas, host and options callbacks, protobuf parsers,
Polly policies. A **Known call** never ran the user's code, so no entry could describe any of them.
What a library does with a caller's delegate is a question about executions — does it run the
delegate now, when a sequence is enumerated, when a member of some object is called, while the host
starts, or somewhere the analysis cannot see — and the engine already models every one of those.

The decision is that library semantics are data, and that most of the data is computed rather than
written:

- A **Library model** describes one member of one assembly version: what it does to each argument
  (none, **Deep read**, write), what it returns, and, for each delegate it receives, its **Delegate
  fate** — one of the executions the engine already has — with what each of the delegate's
  parameters is handed. What a call returns and what a delegate is handed are written in one small
  recursive language of values: an argument, what a delegate returned, the elements of a value, and
  a new **Library sequence**, grouping, collection or dictionary built from values. So `Where` returns
  a sequence of its source's elements, `Select` one of what its selector returned, `ToDictionary` a
  dictionary keyed by what one delegate returned and holding what the other returned, and each
  delegate is handed the elements of the source. A result the model does not describe is linked to
  nothing, as a known call's result was before. The same values say three more things a member
  does (phase 5d, run A2). It writes the cells of an array — its argument's, or its receiver's for
  an instance member — and may say what it puts there: `Array.Sort` rewrites the cells it reads,
  `Array.Fill` puts its value in every one, `Array.Copy` the source's elements. It assigns its `out`
  and `ref` arguments: `Array.Resize` a new array holding the old one's elements. It leaves values
  with an object and hands them back later, as a cache does: `GetOrCreate` keeps what its factory
  returned with the cache and returns that or anything kept there before, `Set` keeps its value, and
  `TryGetValue` assigns what is kept to its `out` argument. What an object keeps is a **Kept
  object**, reachable from its keeper, so a cache that is shared shares it. A keeper the heap has no
  object for — a cache the framework registers where the analysis cannot see — keeps into one store
  for each type, shared by the process scope. And a result may be a new object whose whole graph is
  new, as a deserializer's is: each field of a source type holds a new object along each access
  path, up to the summaries' depth. `di-factory` needs the service and the lifetime of a
  registration, so it comes with the generator, which derives it from a registration it sees. Models
  come in **Model layers** with provenance: built-in
  (shipped in the executable), project (written by the team in the repository), generated (by the
  **Model generator**) and AI. A project entry overrides every other layer, including by declaring
  a member opaque. Hand-written entries may name overloads by pattern; a lock file pins the exact
  declaration ids, so resolution stays by exact symbol and version (TD-122).
- The **Model generator** decompiles the library with ICSharpCode.Decompiler, which ships inside the
  executable as Z3 does (ADR 0004). The decompiled code goes through the analysis's own Roslyn
  frontend: there is no second frontend for libraries. For each member it writes a **Driver** — a
  small program whose action calls the member with probe lambdas — and reads where each probe's
  write lands: at the call, on enumeration of the result, or at a call of a member of the object
  that keeps the delegate. Drivers are synthesized from the member's signature; nobody writes them.
- Generated and project models live in the target repository, under `.concurrency-hunter/models/`
  next to the suppressions file, and are meant to be committed: a team reviews them, shares them and
  promotes a generated entry to a project entry by editing it. Built-in models cover popular
  packages and are generated by us before a release; the run generates only what is missing, for
  the members it actually reached, within a budget. One hand-written family covers a whole type
  rather than a census: every operator of `System.Linq.Enumerable` that takes a delegate and no
  comparer. They are the most frequent delegate gap, their semantics are documented operator by
  operator, and the generator reads them badly until the engine prunes type tests and reaches a
  library iterator's `MoveNext` (questions 38 and 39).
- The **Open-world rule** governs everything the generator concludes. Library code is not a closed
  world: whoever calls a stored delegate may be framework code no root reaches. A delegate the
  driver did not see run, or saw run and still kept after the call, runs in an **Unknown
  execution**. A delegate is `invoke-now` only when it ran during the call and nothing keeps it
  afterwards, which the heap decides, not the probe. A **Holder** is defined by reachability: a
  delegate reachable only through the object that keeps it runs wherever any member of that object
  runs; the triggers the driver happened to observe are information, never the whole list.
- AI models answer what neither the code nor the driver shows — mostly when a callback runs relative
  to startup and requests, and how often a DI factory runs. Only a model class shown to be
  calibrated on the gold set may produce them. A model from a non-manual layer may remove pairs the
  **Unknown effect** of that call would have made; coverage counts, per layer, the pairs each layer
  removed.

The research behind this measured each step on the 49 members behind eShop's delegate gaps, labelled
by hand and verified against the libraries' sources. Decompiled code compiles under Roslyn with
99.6–100% of method bodies free of errors, EF Core included. The engine on decompiled Polly placed a
retry callback in the request that executes the policy and found the `Task.Run` inside a
pessimistic timeout — semantics that depend on how the policy was configured, which no table can
express. Drivers synthesized from signatures compiled for all 131 members sampled from protobuf,
`System.Security.Claims`, Polly and LINQ, and their definite labels agreed with an independent
reading of the decompiled code on 125 of 131.

Rejected: hand-written families, the phase 5a format. They do not scale and they cannot describe
delegates without a vocabulary that is itself execution semantics. Rejected: an IL frontend of our
own. It is a second frontend to keep equivalent with the first, and it must rebuild what the
decompiler already reconstructs — lambdas, closures, `async` state machines — before it can answer
the one question it is good at, which is where a delegate goes. Rejected: a library's published sources
in place of its decompiled code. They are built with conditional compilation, generated code and
internal attributes, and the assembly installed is another build, whose MVID the model is bound to;
tying the two together is work the decompiled code never needs. And decompilation does not cost what
the sources would buy: `System.Linq` 8.0.31 leaves 5 of 853 bodies `extern`, `System.Security.Claims`
0 of 125, Polly 7.2.3 0 of 978, Google.Protobuf 3.21.9 1 of 2,623 and `System.Private.CoreLib` 8.0.31
155 of 30,736, the bodies of `Unsafe`, which the runtime replaces anyway, among them, and no model eval's
inexact fate comes from decompilation. Rejected: analysing library bodies
as source inside every run. One Polly call grew the reachable bodies from 7 to about 150, and a
stored delegate that only the framework invokes silently stopped running: the protobuf parser
factory lost its finding with no gap and no counter. Rejected: models written by AI from the
signature and documentation alone. A calibrated model came close on famous packages, where it has
read the code, and a weaker one labelled retry callbacks `invoke-now` with confidence 0.85; the
code, not the documentation, has to be the input. Rejected: trusting the triggers a driver
observed. For a circuit breaker the driver saw `Isolate` break the circuit and missed `Execute`,
which breaks it on a failure; a model built on that list would have lost every race between the
callback and the requests that run the policy. Rejected: a single effect, `returns-arg`, for what a
call returns, as question 29 first asked. It says that `Take` yields its source's elements, but not
that `Select` yields what its selector returned, what a `ToDictionary` holds as keys and as values, or
what a `GroupBy` group holds. Rejected: handing each delegate parameter whatever of its type the
call's arguments reach. It needs no data, but it guesses at the library the model exists to
describe, and it cannot say where a delegate's result goes. Rejected (run A2): a result marked
shared, with no store behind it. It makes the object `GetOrCreate` returns shared, but a value one
request puts in with `Set` and another takes out with `Get` stays unlinked, which is the common
case of a cache. Rejected: a cache modelled as a dictionary with keys. It would tell two keys apart,
but a library object's keys are values the heap has to track through the caller's code, and a store
per keeper answers the question that matters — who can reach what was kept. Rejected: an undescribed
result read as an unknown shared object. It is the open-world answer, but it adds an object to every
known call's result and moves every finding set at once; a model says `new` where the result is a
new object, and an undescribed result stays linked to nothing. Keepers the heap cannot tell apart
share one store per type, which may join two caches that are in fact different; that is a false
pair at worst, where a store per call site would have missed every value one site kept and another
read.

The consequences to hold. The plugin now writes to the repository, and only there: generated
models under `.concurrency-hunter/models/`, never a source file, project file or build output. The
cold performance targets are revised with generation in them. The engine's precision on library
code becomes product behaviour: a type test it does not prune or a factory-built receiver it loses
turns a precise model into an unknown execution, which is safe but costs findings. A decompiler bug
is silent when the result compiles; a member whose body does not compile is left opaque and
counted. A decompiled library runs through the same lowering as user code, so a defect the
generator hits there is a defect in user code too.

## Amendment, 2026-10-17: the built-in CoreLib models describe the members programs call

Question 85 extended the built-in models from popular packages to every public member of
`System.Private.CoreLib`, generated once per supported major version of .NET, and ADR 0019 and ADR 0022
made that generation possible and repeatable. The first generation of every member took 1 h 45 min at a
peak of 5.1 GiB and gave models to 557 of 19,370 members. Loaded as built-in models, they moved nothing:
eShop's 36 findings and the demo's 261 kept their fingerprints, accesses, pair candidates and semantic
gaps, and one and ten more calls became known. Of eShop's 2,881 calls of library members, 374 opaque ones
call CoreLib: 184 a member of a type a recognizer owns, for which no model is ever read; 113 an interface
or abstract member, for which the generator synthesizes no driver; 45 a member whose parameters can hold
no object of the program; 31 a member the generator stops on or refuses; one a member with a model. The
other 1,791 opaque calls go to other assemblies — IdentityServer, Serilog, ASP.NET Core MVC, configuration,
`System.Security.Claims`, protobuf. The CoreLib semantic gaps of both corpora, `CancellationToken.Register`,
`AssemblyName.Name`, `FieldInfo.SetValue`, `Random.NextBytes` and `CollectionsMarshal.SetCount`, are all
members the generator stops on or refuses.

The decision is that the built-in models of `System.Private.CoreLib` describe the members programs call,
not the assembly:

- The members are taken by census, as a hand-written family's are: the CoreLib members met among the
  metadata calls of the demo and the corpora, less the members of a type a recognizer owns. The generator
  runs over that list for each supported major version, and its models are the built-in generated ones.
- A member of the list that gets no generated model and takes a delegate or leaves a gap in a corpus gets
  a hand-written built-in entry. `CancellationToken.Register` is the first.
- Every other CoreLib member is an opaque call, as it is in a program without a model for it.
- The generation of every public member stays the measure of what a change of the generator or the engine
  moves (ADR 0022); nothing that ships waits on its refusals. A refusal the generator gives a member of the
  list — a culture stand-in, `overridable`, a `ref` argument — is worked on when that member needs it.

Rejected: generating every member, as question 85 decided. A regeneration costs two hours per major version,
each family of refusals is a prerequisite of its own — the last two, questions 144 and 142, gave 11 models
and none — and the result moved no finding on either corpus. Rejected: no CoreLib models at all. The
corpora's CoreLib gaps are delegates and objects handed to members the generator stops on, and one
hand-written entry each describes them. Rejected: generating CoreLib members inside the run, as a package's
are. A CoreLib member meets the closure bound far more often than a package's (ADR 0019), and every cold run
would pay for it.

The consequence to hold. The snapshot of the generation names a member by its classic declaration id, and
the run looks a member up by the id with its return type, so an entry taken from the snapshot is never found
until it is written in the run's form (question 179).

## Amendment, 2026-10-17: the run generates the members it reached

Before the run's generated layer was built, the generator was run one member at a time on every member
outside `System.Private.CoreLib` whose opaque call the demo or eShop reaches: 52 members and 473. The demo
got one model and eShop six; two of them describe a delegate — the protobuf parser's factory as
`unknown-execution`, Autofac's service provider factory as a `holder`. Of eShop's members, 115 had no
implementation because the generator does not look in the ASP.NET Core shared framework, and 123 belong
to libraries that did not compile, IdentityServer's 83 among them, mostly with namespaces and types
missing (CS0234, CS0246), which is what a package built on ASP.NET Core gets when that framework is not
among its references; 53 got no driver, 53 failed in analysis and 39 handed a probe to code the analysis
cannot see. A member took 3 s at the median and 11 s at the 90th percentile. Four `LoggerConfiguration`
members of Serilog and one of IdentityModel ran past 600 s, and five members of EF Core overflowed the
stack while their driver was being synthesized: seed and witness classes were written for each other
without end. Generating eShop's members one after another took 89 minutes.

The decision is how the run generates:

- The run generates the members it reached that no layer describes and writes what the generator
  answered to `.concurrency-hunter/models/generated/<package>/<version>/<mvid>.json` under the
  **Repository root**, creating the folder when the repository has none. A team that never asked for the
  layer finds the folder after its first run; that is the price of a layer that works without setup, and
  the files are what FR-21 asks the team to commit.
- A file keeps the generator's answer about each member: its model, or a **Generation refusal** with the
  cause. A later run reads it and generates nothing that has an answer. A file keeps nothing that depends
  on the run or the machine: a member the run's budget did not reach, a run that stopped, an
  implementation that is not on disk. The run adds files and entries and never deletes a file: a run sees
  one solution, and a repository may hold several.
- A generated model of a package's member belongs to the package's assembly by name, version and MVID.
  One of a shared framework's member belongs to the assembly by name and version within the framework's
  major version, as `generated/<framework>/<major>.0/<assembly>.json`: the implementation of a shared
  framework is the patch installed on the machine, and binding it by MVID would make every machine with
  another patch generate the member again and write a file of its own. A model is not yet bound to the
  generator's version either, so a model an older generator wrote, or one written against another patch,
  stays until its file is removed; binding to the generator's version is run B3b's.
- The **Generation budget** is two limits of time, the run's and each member's. A member that reaches its
  own limit is refused with `timeout` and is not generated again; the members the run's limit does not
  reach stay opaque in that run. Members handed a delegate come first, then the rest by id. The values
  are placeholders until run C measures generation on eShop.
- Generation runs in the server's own process and stops a member at its limit by cancellation. The
  recursion that overflowed the stack is fixed, because an overflow cannot be caught and would end the
  run.
- The pairs a generated model removed are counted by analysing again, with the generated layer off, every
  scope in which that layer described a call; the count is the pairs of that analysis the real one does
  not have.
- The generator reads the ASP.NET Core shared framework, as the implementation of its own members and as
  a reference of the packages built on it.
- Inside a generation, a call of another library's member that has no model stays opaque: generation
  does not follow dependencies yet. That is run B4b's, after the generator's precision.

Rejected: generating only where `.concurrency-hunter/models/` exists. It changes no one's run, but no
team gets a model it did not ask for. Rejected: generating in memory and writing only where the folder
exists. Every cold run without the folder pays again, and on eShop that is 89 minutes. Rejected: keeping
models only. Every refused member — most of them — is generated again in every run. Rejected: keeping
every outcome. A member the budget did not reach would stay unanswered for good. Rejected: one budget for
the whole run. One slow member spends it, in every run. Rejected: a budget counted in steps of the engine.
It would answer alike on every machine, but the engine has no such counter. Rejected: generating in a
child process. A crash or a hang would be one member's refusal, at the cost of a protocol between the two
processes; the measured crash is one fixable recursion. Rejected: estimating the removed pairs from the
**Unknown effect** at the call alone. It misses the pairs that effect makes through the heap — an argument
that escapes, a delegate run in an **Unknown execution** — and undercounts the one number that keeps the
narrowing visible. Rejected: binding a model to the plugin's version, which has stayed 0.1.0 while the
generator changed, or to the build, which would regenerate every model on every rebuild.

The consequence to hold. Until the generator describes more members, the layer moves few findings: it would
describe one member the demo calls and six that eShop calls. The demo commits its generated files, and a test fails
rather than let a demo run generate.
